DATA ENGINEERING / FIELD NOTE

A dataset is not a finished product. It is an opening statement.

Nandini Thakur · 2 min read

The pipeline finished. Excellent. Now comes the small matter of whether someone can use what came out of it.

The engineering questions that interest me extend beyond moving data from one place to another. I want to know what the records mean, where they came from, and whether the next person can tell when something has gone wrong.

Make the next person’s job possible

For a dataset I would hand to someone else, I’d want a clear owner, an explanation of its fields, a trace back to its source, and a statement of its freshness and known limitations. A table named final_v3_really_final communicates a journey. It does not communicate a contract.

I find the idea of treating data as a product useful here: discoverability, understandable semantics, and trustworthiness are part of what makes data usable. Zhamak Dehghani’s writing on data mesh is a good starting point for that perspective.

My question before the next layer

If I build a model or a financial research tool on top of this dataset, what am I assuming about it? Can I check those assumptions? Would I notice a change? Those are the questions I want my engineering decisions to make easier to answer.

Moving the data is work. Making it understandable is also work. I’d like both parts to appear in the definition of done.

Further reading: Zhamak Dehghani — data as a product ↗
Still thinking this through. A good counterargument is welcome.
